Tan Mei Lin and the Kuala Lumpur bank are fictional; the data is synthetic.

Hook.voiceover: A sales manager asks, your model says who will subscribe, so why those people? If your only answer is the algorithm decided, she will not trust it, and she should not. Today you learn three ways to see which features drive a model.

Explain.voiceover: The first way is coefficients, which you met in lesson six. For linear and logistic models, they show the direction and size of each feature's effect, if the features are scaled. They are simple, but they only exist for linear models.

slide.title: 1. Coefficients
slide.body: Linear and logistic models only · Direction and size of each effect, after scaling · Related features can share weight in confusing ways

Explain.voiceover: The second way is tree feature importances, in random forests and many tree models. They measure how much each feature improved the splits while the trees were built. They are quick, but they have some known limits, so check them against the third way.

slide.title: 2. Tree feature importances
slide.body: feature_importances_ in tree models · How much each feature improved the splits · Quick, but check with permutation importance

Explain.voiceover: The third way is permutation importance, and it works with any model, including a whole pipeline. It takes one column at a time, shuffles its values randomly, and measures how much the score drops. If the score falls a lot, the model relies on that column. If it barely moves, the model does not need it.

slide.title: 3. Permutation importance
slide.body: Table with one column shuffled (arrows mixing its values) → score before vs after → drop = importance. Run on held-out data; one number per original column, e.g. 'job'.

Explain.voiceover: Three limits apply to all of these. Importance is not cause. Changing a feature does not necessarily change the outcome. Correlated features share importance, so if two columns carry the same information, both may look unimportant. And importance describes this model on this data, not the world in general.

slide.title: Three limits
slide.body: Importance ≠ cause · Correlated features share importance · Describes this model on this data only

Explain.voiceover: Permutation importance is like muting the instruments in a band, one at a time. If the song falls apart without the drums, the drums matter. But if two guitars play the same part, muting either one changes little, and you might wrongly decide that neither guitar matters.
Explain.on_screen_text: Mute one instrument at a time

Demonstrate.voiceover: Tan Mei Lin is a data scientist at a bank in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. She must explain the term-deposit model to the sales team. She continues in the bank notebook, where the logistic regression pipeline is fitted.
Demonstrate.stock_query: data scientist presenting to sales team
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Mei Lin · data scientist · Kuala Lumpur

Demonstrate.voiceover: This cell runs permutation importance on the test set, scored by ROC AUC. It shuffles each original column twenty times, and records the average drop and its spread. Then it prints the columns sorted from most to least important.
screen_steps: Scroll past the L05 setup and pipeline cells, already executed.

Type this exact code cell from content.md and run it with Shift+Enter:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
import pandas as pd

result = permutation_importance(pipe, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc",
                                n_repeats=20, random_state=42)
imp = pd.DataFrame({"mean": result.importances_mean, "std": result.importances_std},
                   index=X_test.columns)
print(imp.sort_values("mean", ascending=False).round(3))

Demonstrate.voiceover: Shuffling the number of calls lowers ROC AUC by about zero point zero seven eight on average. That is the largest drop. Age follows closely at zero point zero six six, and job at zero point zero six five.
screen_steps: Highlight the rows calls 0.078, age 0.066 and job 0.065.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Contact type drops the score by zero point zero three zero. Balance has a mean drop of zero point zero one one, with a spread of zero point zero one two. The spread is larger than the mean, so its effect cannot be separated from zero with this test set.
screen_steps: Highlight the row balance 0.011 0.012 and label it 'no clear effect'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then Mei Lin writes three sentences for the sales manager. One. The number of times we have already called a customer in this campaign is the strongest signal. Customers called many times are less likely to subscribe.
screen_steps: Add a text cell and type sentence 1 from content.md.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Plain words for the sales team

Demonstrate.voiceover: Two. Age and job type matter almost as much. Older and retired customers are more likely to say yes. Three. Account balance adds very little once we know the other information. These are patterns in past data, not proof that calling less will make people subscribe.
screen_steps: Type sentences 2 and 3 from content.md in the same text cell.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The most common mistake is to present importance as cause, for example, reduce calls and subscriptions will rise. The model only shows that customers with many calls subscribed less in the past. Perhaps the bank kept calling people who were never interested.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, coefficients, tree importances and permutation importance each show which features a model relies on, with different strengths and limits. Second, permutation importance works with any pipeline, and should be run on held-out data, with its spread reported. Third, importance is not cause, so say is linked with, and watch for correlated features that share importance.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Coefficients · tree importances · permutation importance. 2. Permutation importance on held-out data, with spread. 3. 'Is linked with', not 'causes'.
